{{Short description|Mathematical problem solved in 1967}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''common fixed point problem''' is the conjecture that, for any two [[continuous function]]s that map the [[unit interval]] into itself and commute under [[Function composition|functional composition]], there must be a point that is a [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] of both functions. In other words, if the functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are continuous, and <math>f(g(x)) = g(f(x))</math> for all <math>x</math> in the unit interval, then there must be some <math>x</math> in the unit interval for which <math>f(x) = x = g(x)</math>. 

First posed in 1954, the problem remained unsolved for more than a decade, during which several mathematicians made incremental progress toward an affirmative answer. In 1967, [[William Martin Boyce|William M. Boyce]] and John P. Huneke independently{{r|:0|p=3}} proved the conjecture to be false by providing examples of commuting functions on a closed interval that do not have a common fixed point.

== History ==
A 1951 paper by H. D. Block and H. P. Thielman sparked interest in the subject of fixed points of commuting functions.<ref name="mcdowell">{{Cite journal |last=McDowell |first=Eric L. |date=5 August 2009 |title=Coincidence Values of Commuting Functions |url=https://topology.nipissingu.ca/tp/reprints/v34/tp34025.pdf |journal=Topology Proceedings |volume=34 |pages=365–384}}</ref> Building on earlier work by [[Joseph Ritt|J. F. Ritt]] and [[Arthur Geoffrey Walker|A. G. Walker]], Block and Thielman identified sets of pairwise commuting polynomials and studied their properties. They proved, for each of these sets, that any two polynomials would share a common fixed point.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=H. D. |last1=Block |first2=H. P. |last2=Thielman |title=Commutative polynomials |journal=The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics |volume=2 |issue=1 |date=1951 |pages=241–243 |doi=10.1093/qmath/2.1.241 }}</ref>

Block and Thielman's paper led other mathematicians to wonder if having a common fixed point was a [[universal property]] of commuting functions. In 1954, Eldon Dyer asked whether if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are two continuous functions that map a closed interval on the [[Number line|real line]] into itself and commute, they must have a common fixed point. The same question was raised independently by [[Allen Shields]] in 1955 and again by [[Lester Dubins]] in 1956.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Shields |first=Allen L. |date=1964 |title=On Fixed Points of Commuting Analytical Functions |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1964-015-05/S0002-9939-1964-0165508-3/S0002-9939-1964-0165508-3.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |volume=15 |issue=5 |pages=703–706 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0165508-3}}</ref> [[John R. Isbell]] also raised the question in a more general form in 1957.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Baxter |first=Glenn |date=December 1964 |title=On Fixed Points of the Composite of Commuting Functions |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1964-015-06/S0002-9939-1964-0184217-8/S0002-9939-1964-0184217-8.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |volume=15 |issue=6 |pages=851–855 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0184217-8}}</ref>

During the 1960s, mathematicians were able to prove that the commuting function conjecture held when certain assumptions were made about <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>.<ref name="mcdowell"/><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Robert F. |date=15 January 2021 |title=A Good Question Won't Go Away: An Example Of Mathematical Research |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=128 |issue=1 |pages=62–68 |doi=10.1080/00029890.2021.1847592}}</ref>

In 1963, Ralph DeMarr showed that if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are both [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]], and if the Lipschitz constant of both is <math>\geq 1</math>, then <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> will have a common fixed point.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=DeMarr |first=Ralph |date=1963 |title=A common fixed point theorem for commuting mappings |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=70 |issue=5 |pages=535–537 |doi=10.2307/2312067|jstor=2312067 }}</ref> Gerald Jungck refined DeMarr's conditions, showing that they need not be Lipschitz continuous, but instead satisfy similar but less restrictive criteria.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jungck |first=Gerald |date=1966 |title=Commuting Mappings and Common Fixed Points |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236595690 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=73 |issue=7 |pages=735–738 |doi=10.2307/2313982|jstor=2313982 }}</ref>

Taking a different approach, Haskell Cohen showed in 1964 that <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> will have a common fixed point if both are continuous and "full", where a continuous function that maps the unit interval into itself is called full if its domain can be split into a finite number of segments, such that for each segment the function [[Restriction (mathematics)|restricted]] to that segment is a [[homeomorphism]] onto the unit interval.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=Haskell |date=1964 |title=On Fixed Points of Commuting Functions |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1964-015-02/S0002-9939-1964-0184219-1/S0002-9939-1964-0184219-1.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=293–296 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1964-0184219-1}}</ref> Later, both [[Jon Folkman|Jon H. Folkman]] and James T. Joichi, working independently, extended Cohen's work, showing that it is only necessary for one of the two functions to be full.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Folkman |first=Jon H. |date=1966 |title=On functions that commute with full functions |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1966-017-02/S0002-9939-1966-0190916-6/S0002-9939-1966-0190916-6.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=383–386 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1966-0190916-6 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Joichi |first=James T. |date=1966 |title=On functions that commute with full functions and common fixed points |journal=Nieuw. Arch. Wiss. |volume=14 |pages=247–251}}</ref>

John Maxfield and W. J. Mourant, in 1965, proved that commuting functions on the unit interval have a common fixed point if one of the functions has no period 2 points (i.e., <math>f(f(x)) = x</math> implies <math>f(x) = x</math>).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maxfield |first1=J. |last2=Mourant |first2=W. |date=1965 |title=Common Fixed Points of Commuting Continuous Functions on the Unit Interval |url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82466882.pdf |journal=Indag. Math. |volume=27 |pages=668–670 |doi=10.1016/S1385-7258(65)50068-8}}</ref> The following year, Sherwood Chu and R. D. Moyer found that the conjecture holds when there is a subinterval in which one of the functions has a fixed point and the other has no period 2 points.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chu |first1=S. |last2=Moyer |first2=R. |date=1966 |title=On Continuous Functions, Commuting Functions and Fixed Points |url=http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm59/fm5919.pdf |journal=Fund. Math. |volume=59 |pages=91–95 |doi=10.4064/fm-59-1-91-95}}</ref>

== Boyce's counterexample ==
William M. Boyce earned his Ph.D. from Tulane University in 1967.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Math Dissertations |url=https://library.tulane.edu/locations/math/math-dissertations |access-date=15 October 2024 |website=Tulane University}}</ref> In his thesis, Boyce identified a pair of functions that commute under composition, but do not have a common fixed point, proving the fixed point conjecture to be false.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boyce |first=William M. |date=March 1969 |title=Commuting Functions with No Common Fixed Point |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1969-137-00/S0002-9947-1969-0236331-5/S0002-9947-1969-0236331-5.pdf |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=137 |pages=77–92 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0236331-5}}</ref>

In 1963, [[Glen E. Baxter|Glenn Baxter]] and Joichi published a paper about the fixed points of the composite function <math>h(x) = f(g(x)) = g(f(x))</math>. It was known that the functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> permute the fixed points of <math>h</math>. Baxter and Joichi noted that at each fixed point, the graph of <math>h</math> must either cross the diagonal going up (an "up-crossing"), or cross it going down (a "down-crossing"), or not cross it but touch the diagonal and then move away in the opposite direction.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baxter |first1=Glen |last2=Joichi |first2=J. T. |date=1963 |title=On Permutations Induced by Commuting Functions, and an Embedding Question |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24490218 |journal=Mathematica Scandinavica |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=140–150 |doi=10.7146/math.scand.a-10696 |jstor=24490218 |issn=0025-5521}}</ref> In an independent paper, Baxter proved that the permutations must preserve the type of each fixed point (up-crossing, down-crossing, touching) and that only certain orderings are allowed.<ref name=":2" />

Boyce wrote a [[computer program]] to generate permutations that followed Baxter's rules, which he named "[[Baxter permutation|Baxter permutations]]."<ref name="mcdowell" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=McCroskey |first=Erin J. |title=The Common Fixed Point Problem Expanded [Master's thesis] |publisher=Tennessee Technological University |year=2013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mallows |first=C. L |date=1979-11-01 |title=Baxter permutations rise again |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0097316579900347 |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=394–396 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(79)90034-7 |issn=0097-3165|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His program carefully screened out those that could be trivially shown to have fixed points or were analytically equivalent to other cases. After eliminating more than  97% of the possible permutations through this process, Boyce constructed pairs of commuting functions from the remaining candidates and was able to prove that one such pair, based on a Baxter permutation with 13 points of crossing on the diagonal, had no common fixed point.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Boyce |first=William M. |date=1967 |title=Generation of a Class of Permutations Associated with Commuting Functions |url=https://oeis.org/A001181/a001181_1.pdf |journal=Mathematical Algorithms |volume=2 |pages=19–26}}</ref>

Boyce's paper is one of the earliest examples of a [[computer-assisted proof]].<ref name=":0" /> It was uncommon in the 1960s for mathematicians to rely on computers for research,<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |title=The Influence of Computing on Mathematical Research and Education |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=1974 |editor-last=LaSalle |editor-first=J. P.|editor-link=Joseph P. LaSalle |pages=vii-viii |quote="The computer intelligently used by, as yet, relatively few mathematicians has proved to be an important empirical tool ..."}}</ref> but Boyce, then serving in the Army, had access to computers at [[MIT Lincoln Laboratory]]. Boyce published a separate paper describing his process for generating Baxter permutations, including the [[Fortran|FORTRAN]] [[source code]] of his program.<ref name=":1" />

== Huneke's counterexample ==
John P. Huneke also investigated the common fixed point problem for his Ph.D. at Wesleyan University, which he also received in 1967. In his thesis, Huneke provides two examples of function pairs that commute but have no common fixed points, using two different strategies.<ref name="Huneke dissertation">{{cite thesis |last=Huneke |first=John Philip |date=1967 |title=On Common Fixed Points of Commuting Continuous Functions on a Closed Interval |degree=PhD |publisher=[[Wesleyan University]] |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302265144|id={{ProQuest|302265144}} }}</ref> The first of Huneke's examples is essentially identical to Boyce's, though Huneke arrived at it through a different process.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Huneke |first=John Philip |date=1969 |title=On common fixed points of commuting continuous functions on an interval |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1969-139-00/S0002-9947-1969-0237724-2/S0002-9947-1969-0237724-2.pdf |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=139 |pages=371–381 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0237724-2 |issn=0002-9947}}</ref>

Huneke's solution is based on the [[mountain climbing problem]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Huneke |first=John Philip |date=1969 |title=Mountain climbing |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1969-139-00/S0002-9947-1969-0239013-9/S0002-9947-1969-0239013-9.pdf |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=139 |pages=383–391 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0239013-9 |issn=0002-9947}}</ref> which states that two climbers, climbing separate mountains of equal height, will be able to climb in such a way that they will always be at the same elevation at each point in time. Huneke used this principle to construct sequences of functions that will converge to the [[counterexample]] to the common fixed point problem.<ref name="Huneke dissertation"/>

== Later research ==
Although the discovery of counterexamples by Boyce and Huneke meant that the decade-long pursuit of a proof of the commuting function conjecture was over, it did enable researchers to focus their efforts on investigating under what conditions, in addition to the ones already discovered, the conjecture still might hold true.<ref name="mcdowell" />

Boyce extended the work of Maxfield/Mourant and Chu/Moyer in 1971, showing weaker conditions that allow both of the commuting functions to have period 2 points but still imply that they must have a common fixed point.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boyce |first=William M. |date=1971 |title=Γ-compact maps on an interval and fixed points |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1971-160-00/S0002-9947-1971-0280655-1/S0002-9947-1971-0280655-1.pdf |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=160 |pages=87–102 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1971-0280655-1 |issn=0002-9947}}</ref> His work was later extended by Theodore Mitchell, Julio Cano, and Jacek R. Jachymski.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mitchell |first=Theodore |date=1972 |title=Common fixed-points for equicontinuous semigroups of mappings |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1972-033-01/S0002-9939-1972-0289735-4/S0002-9939-1972-0289735-4.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=146–150 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1972-0289735-4 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cano |first=J. |date=1982 |title=Common fixed points for a class of commuting mappings on an interval |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1982-086-02/S0002-9939-1982-0667301-2/S0002-9939-1982-0667301-2.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=86 |issue=2 |pages=336–338 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1982-0667301-2 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jachymski |first=Jacek |date=1996 |title=Equivalent conditions involving common fixed points for maps on the unit interval |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1996-124-10/S0002-9939-96-03397-7/S0002-9939-96-03397-7.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=124 |issue=10 |pages=3229–3233 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-96-03397-7 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref>

Over 25 years after the publication of his first paper, Jungck defined additional conditions under which <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> will have a common fixed point, based on the notions of periodic points and the coincidence set of the functions, that is, the values for which <math>f(x) = g(x)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jungck |first=Gerald |date=1992 |title=Common fixed points for compatible maps on the unit interval |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1992-115-02/S0002-9939-1992-1105040-0/S0002-9939-1992-1105040-0.pdf |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=115 |issue=2 |pages=495–499 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1992-1105040-0 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref>

[[Baxter permutation|Baxter permutations]] have become a subject of research in their own right and have been applied to other problems beyond the common fixed point problem.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chung |first1=F. R. K. |author1-link=Fan Chung |last2=Graham |first2=R. L. |author2-link=Ronald Graham |last3=Hoggatt |first3=V. E. Jr. |author3-link=Verner Emil Hoggatt Jr. |last4=Kleiman |first4=M. |date=1978 |title=The number of Baxter permutations |url=http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/78_08_baxter.pdf |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] |series=Series A |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=382–394 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(78)90068-7 |doi-access=free |mr=491652 |quote=Baxter permutations apparently first arose in attempts to prove the "commuting function" conjecture&nbsp;... However,&nbsp;... Baxter permutations are of more general significance in analysis than had previously been realized.}}</ref>
